mcqs.q: Chronic hepatitis is defined as inflammation of the liver lasting:
mcqs.explain: Chronic hepatitis is any hepatitis lasting 6 months or longer; chronic viral hepatitis is the principal cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide.

mcqs.q: Which hepatitis viruses are transmitted by the FECO-ORAL route?
mcqs.explain: HAV and HEV spread feco-orally and do not become chronic; HBV, HCV and HDV are blood-borne and can become chronic.

mcqs.q: The genome of hepatitis B virus is:
mcqs.explain: HBV is the only DNA hepatitis virus; HAV, HCV, HDV and HEV are RNA viruses.

mcqs.q: In the dental office, hepatitis B is most commonly transmitted via:
opts: Saliva, needle-prick injuries and blood of carriers
mcqs.explain: In dentistry, HBV is mostly transmitted via saliva, needle-prick injuries and blood, and is present in gingival crevicular fluid.

mcqs.q: Compared with vaccinated colleagues, unvaccinated dental health-care workers have a hepatitis B infection risk that is about:
mcqs.explain: Unvaccinated dental staff have a 10× greater risk of HBV infection because of occupational exposure — hence the importance of vaccination.

mcqs.q: Which statement about hepatitis C is correct?
opts: There is no protective vaccine, and infection persists in about 80%
mcqs.explain: HCV has no vaccine; acute disease is usually mild but persists in ~80%, of whom ~20% develop cirrhosis, with a ~10% risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

mcqs.q: Hepatitis C is most commonly associated with:
mcqs.explain: HCV is commoner in IV drug users and with tattooing; it is less readily transmitted during dentistry and is more vulnerable to antiseptics.

mcqs.q: A recognised oral manifestation associated with hepatitis B and C is:
mcqs.explain: Lichen planus, Sjögren's syndrome and sialadenitis are associated with HBV/HCV; some oral cancers may also occur.

mcqs.q: Spontaneous petechiae or excessive gingival bleeding in a hepatitis patient is especially suggestive of liver disease when it occurs:
opts: In the absence of gingival inflammation
mcqs.explain: Impaired haemostasis (thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism/interferon) causes petechiae and gingival bleeding — especially suggestive when there is no inflammation.

mcqs.q: Which serological marker confirms hepatitis C infection?
mcqs.explain: HCV is diagnosed by anti-HCV antibody and HCV-RNA; HBsAg indicates HBV, and IgM anti-HAV/anti-HEV indicate HAV/HEV.

mcqs.q: The hepatitis B vaccine is best described as:
opts: Safe, effective and protective for life
mcqs.explain: The HBV vaccine is safe and effective and protects for a lifetime; all dental health-care workers (and patients) should be vaccinated.

mcqs.q: When treating a known hepatitis carrier, aerosol-generating risk is reduced by:
opts: Avoiding ultrasonics, air syringe and high-speed handpieces, and pre-rinsing with chlorhexidine
mcqs.explain: Saliva carries the virus, so avoid ultrasonics/air syringe/high-speed handpieces and pre-rinse with chlorhexidine gluconate for 30 seconds.

mcqs.q: On environmental surfaces, hepatitis B virus can survive for at least:
mcqs.explain: HBV can survive on surfaces for at least one week and HCV for more than five days, so thorough surface disinfection is essential.

mcqs.q: The CDC-recommended bleach dilution for cleaning exposed surfaces is:
mcqs.explain: The CDC recommends a 1:10 dilution of bleach to water; surfaces may also be wiped with 2% activated glutaraldehyde (Cidex).

mcqs.q: The FIRST step after a needlestick exposure is to:
opts: Wash the site with soap and water (no caustics or antiseptics in the wound)
Rinse the wound with strong disinfectant
Ignore it until the next day
mcqs.explain: Wash the exposure site with soap and water (mucosa/eyes with water only); do not use caustics or rinse the wound with antiseptics/disinfectants.

mcqs.q: After an exposure in an unvaccinated person, hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) should ideally be given:
opts: As soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours
mcqs.explain: HBIG should be given as soon as possible (preferably within 24 h) and the HBV vaccine series started (0, 1, 6 months) at a separate site.

mcqs.q: The hepatitis B vaccination series is given on the schedule:
mcqs.explain: The HBV vaccine series is given at 0, 1 and 6 months; anti-HBs antibodies are tested 1–2 months after the last dose.

mcqs.q: An HBV-infected dental provider may perform exposure-prone procedures if the HBV viral load is kept below:
opts: 1000 IU/mL, with testing at least every six months
mcqs.explain: An HBV-infected provider can perform exposure-prone procedures with a documented low/undetectable viral load — a threshold of 1000 IU/mL, retested at least every six months.

mcqs.q: Which hepatitis virus REQUIRES co-infection with HBV to replicate?
mcqs.explain: HDV is a defective (viroid) virus that needs HBV; therefore HBV vaccination also prevents HDV.

mcqs.q: Acute hepatitis can be caused by:
mcqs.explain: Acute parenchymal liver damage (acute hepatitis) can be caused by many agents — viruses, toxins and drugs.

mcqs.q: Which carrier state pattern is correct?
opts: HBV has a carrier state; HAV does not
HAV has a carrier state; HBV does not
Neither HAV nor HBV has a carrier state
Only HEV has a carrier state
mcqs.explain: HBV (and HDV) have carrier states and can become chronic; HAV and HEV do not have a carrier state and do not become chronic.

mcqs.q: When a hepatitis carrier needs emergency dental treatment and bleeding is likely, you should:
opts: Consult the physician and measure PT and bleeding time
Give the HBV vaccine during the appointment to treat it
mcqs.explain: Consult the patient's physician about their status and, if bleeding is likely, measure PT and bleeding time, while using full barrier technique.

mcqs.q: During treatment of an infectious patient, all personnel in clinical contact should use:
opts: Full barrier technique — mask, gloves, eye protection and gown
mcqs.explain: Full barrier technique (masks, gloves, glasses/eye shields and disposable gowns) plus aseptic technique should be used throughout.

mcqs.q: Where are HCV-RNA levels typically highest in an infected patient's mouth?
opts: The gingival sulcus (higher than in saliva)
mcqs.explain: Most HCV patients have higher HCV-RNA levels in the gingival sulcus than in saliva, and HCV-RNA can even be found on their toothbrushes.

saqs.q: Distinguish acute from chronic hepatitis and state its global importance.
saqs.a: Acute: parenchymal liver damage from viruses/toxins/drugs. Chronic: hepatitis lasting ≥6 months. Chronic viral hepatitis is the principal cause of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide.

saqs.q: Compare the transmission and chronicity of the five hepatitis viruses.
saqs.a: HAV & HEV: feco-oral, no chronicity. HBV (DNA), HCV, HDV: blood-borne (HBV/HCV also saliva), can become chronic. HBV/HDV have carrier states.

saqs.q: Why is hepatitis B a major occupational risk in dentistry?
saqs.a: It is present in saliva, blood and gingival crevicular fluid and spreads via needle-prick injuries; unvaccinated dental staff have a 10× greater risk of infection. HBV survives surfaces ≥1 week.

saqs.q: Summarise the key features of hepatitis C.
saqs.a: RNA virus, no vaccine; usually mild acute illness but persists in 80% (20% → cirrhosis), ~10% HCC risk. Commoner in IV drug users/tattooing; HCV-RNA highest in the gingival sulcus.

saqs.q: List the oral manifestations associated with viral hepatitis.
saqs.a: Lichen planus, Sjögren's syndrome, sialadenitis, some oral cancers, and (in cirrhosis) petechiae/gingival bleeding from thrombocytopenia — especially without inflammation.

saqs.q: Outline infection-control measures for a hepatitis carrier in the dental office.
saqs.a: Full barrier technique, aseptic technique, minimise aerosols (avoid ultrasonics/air syringe/high-speed), chlorhexidine pre-rinse 30 s; sterilise/dispose instruments; surfaces with 1:10 bleach or 2% glutaraldehyde.

saqs.q: Describe post-exposure prophylaxis after a needlestick injury.
saqs.a: 1. Wash the site with soap & water (no antiseptics in wound). 2. Report/document. 3. Evaluate the source (HBsAg, HCV, HIV, viral load). 4. Prophylaxis: HBV vaccine series (0,1,6 mo) if unvaccinated + HBIG within 24 h.
